question: So does a Signal block an unsafe answer before the user receives it, or is that something my agent must do separately?

conversation_context.content: How do tracing, evaluations, and Signals fit together?

I reached this turn's research limit without a draft passing all checks. Research may be incomplete, or the verifier may have rejected a useful draft; this does not establish that the docs lack an answer. Inspect the trace for the stopping reason.

answer:
**Short answer: the docs I read describe Signals as monitoring that happens after a turn, and they don't document Signals blocking a response. For stopping an unsafe answer before the user sees it, the documented mechanism is a guardrail, which you add to your application code.**

**What Signals are documented to do**
- Signals show tags and ratings on your agent's conversations. They "surface quality and safety issues to flag problems, find patterns, and highlight the traces that need your attention" [S1]. The page doesn't describe blocking or changing a response.
- For remote-scorer Signals, the documented flow starts when a turn ends. A root span ending emits a `weave.genai.turn_ended` event. A scoring worker then loads the active signals and writes the result as feedback on the turn [S12]. That page also says scoring is asynchronous, so results appear after a delay [S13]. I only read this flow for remote scorers. I didn't confirm it for other Signal types.
- Because scoring is triggered by a finished turn, I wouldn't rely on a Signal as a pre-delivery check. That is my inference from the documented flow. It isn't an explicit statement in the docs.

**What the docs say about blocking**
- Weave documents guardrails separately. They use inline Weave Scorers to assess user input or LLM output and adjust responses in real time. They can block or modify a response when a score crosses a threshold [S10][S14].
- Guardrails require code changes because they affect your application's control flow. Monitors are the alternative if you only want to score traffic passively [S14].
- Guardrail scorer results are also stored in Weave, so they function as monitors too [S14].

**Limits of what I checked**
- I didn't find a page in the searched snapshot that connects guardrails to agent turns or Signals. That doesn't prove no such integration exists.
- I didn't read the guardrail code examples, so I can't describe the exact code pattern.
- The guardrails page says the TypeScript SDK doesn't support the tools needed to set up guardrails [S14].

**Next step:** If you need real-time blocking, read the guardrails guide, including its examples, to see how to add a scorer check to your code. Use Signals for after-the-fact monitoring in the Agents view.

# Monitor your agents with signals

> Use Weave signals to score agent turns, apply tags, and surface quality and safety issues in production.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/tags/create-tag.md).

In Weave's [Agents view](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-activity.md), the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations. Signals surface quality and safety issues to flag problems, find patterns, and highlight the traces that need your attention. Use signals to automatically score the quality of your agent's responses, notice when a user is frustrated, or flag NSFW content.

To score turns with an HTTP endpoint that you host instead of an LLM judge, see [Score agent turns with a remote scorer](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/remote-scorer-signals.md).

sources.title: Score agent turns with a remote scorer
sources.heading: How agent turn scoring works
sources.text:
## How agent turn scoring works

An agent turn is scored in the following sequence:

1. A turn ends. When a root span (a span with no parent) ends, Weave treats it as a completed turn and emits a `weave.genai.turn_ended` event.
2. The agent scoring worker loads the project's active signals that target `weave.genai.turn_ended`, then applies each signal's filters and sample rate.
3. For each `RemoteScorer` on a matching signal, the worker builds a `schema_version: 2` request from the turn's span, including its messages, resolves the scorer's credentials, checks the endpoint URL against the allowed hosts, and sends the `POST`.
4. The worker validates the response and writes the result as feedback on the turn. Tags and ratings appear on the **Signals** tab.

Weave scores only completed turns. Individual LLM and tool spans, and whole conversations, aren't remote scoring targets. A remote scorer signal is a `Monitor` whose `op_names` is `["weave.genai.turn_ended"]`, whether you create it in the UI or with the SDK.

The worker retries a failed attempt with the same `Idempotency-Key`, up to three attempts within 30 seconds of the first attempt. A `5xx`, `408`, or `429` response is retried. A timeout uses the whole 30 seconds, so a timed-out request isn't retried. Any other `4xx` response isn't retried. If your endpoint can't score a turn in time, return `503` quickly rather than letting the request time out, so that Weave retries it. Agent turn scoring requires the structured result format, because Weave stores the tags and ratings as typed feedback columns.

# Score agent turns with a remote scorer

> Score Weave agent turns with your own HTTP endpoint and see the results as tags or ratings on the Signals tab.

A remote scorer signal scores each completed agent turn with an HTTP endpoint that you host, instead of with an LLM judge. When a turn ends, the Weave agent scoring worker sends the turn to your endpoint in an HTTP `POST` and records the response as feedback on the turn. The result appears as a tag or rating on the **Signals** tab of the [Agents view](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-signals.md).

This page covers remote scorers for agent turns. To score Calls traced with `@weave.op`, see [Score Calls with remote scorers](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/remote-scorers.md). You configure remote scorers with the Python SDK or the Weave UI. The TypeScript SDK doesn't include `RemoteScorer`.

sources.heading: Test the signal
sources.text:
## Test the signal

Before you test, deploy the endpoint at an HTTPS URL that's on the allowed hosts, and register it.

Log one completed turn, then check the **Signals** tab. Scoring is asynchronous, so the result appears after a delay.

```python lines theme={"system"}
import uuid

from opentelemetry import trace

import weave
from weave.conversation import Message, log_turn

weave.init("[YOUR-TEAM]/[YOUR-PROJECT]")

result = log_turn(
    conversation_id=f"sample-{uuid.uuid4().hex}",
    agent_name="sample-support-agent",
    system_instructions=["Answer the user accurately and concisely."],
    messages=[Message.user("What are your support hours?")],
    output_messages=[
        Message.assistant(
            "Our support team is available Monday through Friday, 9am to 5pm Eastern."
        )
    ],
)

# weave.init exports spans from a background thread. Flush before a short script exits.
trace.get_tracer_provider().force_flush(30_000)
print(result.conversation_id, result.trace_ids)
```

Your endpoint receives a V2 request with `scoring_target.type` set to `agent_turn`, and Weave records the result as feedback on that turn.

sources.text:
# Set up guardrails

> Ensure LLM safety and measure output quality in production applications

Guardrails intervene in your LLM application's behavior based on scores from LLM judges. They run in real time before outputs reach users and can block or modify responses when scores exceed thresholds. You can use guardrails to block toxic content, filter responses for personally identifiable information (PII), or block abusive input from users.

This guide explains how Weave guardrails work, how to tune their performance, and walks through examples that use built-in scorers, custom scorers, and AWS Bedrock Guardrails to protect production LLM applications.

sources.title: Set up guardrails
sources.heading: How Weave guardrails work
sources.text:
## How Weave guardrails work

Weave guardrails use inline [Weave Scorers](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md) to assess the input from a user or the output from an LLM and adjust the LLM's responses in real time. You can configure custom scorers or use [built-in scorers](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/builtin_scorers.md) to assess content for a variety of purposes. This guide demonstrates how to use both types of scorers as guardrails.

If you want to passively score production traffic without modifying your application's control flow, use [monitors](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/monitors.md) instead.

Unlike monitors, guardrails require code changes because they affect your application's control flow. However, every scorer result from guardrails is automatically stored in Weave's database, so your guardrails also function as monitors without any extra configuration. You can analyze historical scorer results regardless of how they were originally used.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The Weave TypeScript SDK doesn't support the tools required to set up guardrails.

Weave scores only completed turns. Individual LLM and tool spans, and whole conversations, aren't remote scoring targets. A remote scorer signal is a `Monitor` whose `op_names` is `["weave.genai.turn_ended"]`, whether you create it in the UI or with the SDK.

The worker retries a failed attempt with the same `Idempotency-Key`, up to three attempts within 30 seconds of the first attempt. A `5xx`, `408`, or `429` response is retried. A timeout uses the whole 30 seconds, so a timed-out request isn't retried. Any other `4xx` response isn't retried. If your endpoint can't score a turn in time, return `503` quickly rather than letting the request time out, so that Weave retries it. Agent turn scoring requires the structured result format, because Weave stores the tags and ratings as typed feedback columns.

## Test the signal

Before you test, deploy the endpoint at an HTTPS URL that's on the allowed hosts, and register it.

```python lines theme={"system"}
import uuid

from opentelemetry import trace

import weave
from weave.conversation import Message, log_turn

weave.init("[YOUR-TEAM]/[YOUR-PROJECT]")

result = log_turn(
    conversation_id=f"sample-{uuid.uuid4().hex}",
    agent_name="sample-support-agent",
    system_instructions=["Answer the user accurately and concisely."],
    messages=[Message.user("What are your support hours?")],
    output_messages=[
        Message.assistant(
            "Our support team is available Monday through Friday, 9am to 5pm Eastern."
        )
    ],
)

# weave.init exports spans from a background thread. Flush before a short script exits.
trace.get_tracer_provider().force_flush(30_000)
print(result.conversation_id, result.trace_ids)
```

all_read_evidence.heading: How Weave guardrails work
all_read_evidence.text:
## How Weave guardrails work

Weave guardrails use inline [Weave Scorers](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md) to assess the input from a user or the output from an LLM and adjust the LLM's responses in real time. You can configure custom scorers or use [built-in scorers](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/builtin_scorers.md) to assess content for a variety of purposes. This guide demonstrates how to use both types of scorers as guardrails.

If you want to passively score production traffic without modifying your application's control flow, use [monitors](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/monitors.md) instead.

Unlike monitors, guardrails require code changes because they affect your application's control flow. However, every scorer result from guardrails is automatically stored in Weave's database, so your guardrails also function as monitors without any extra configuration. You can analyze historical scorer results regardless of how they were originally used.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The Weave TypeScript SDK doesn't support the tools required to set up guardrails.
all_read_evidence.page_context:
# Set up guardrails

> Ensure LLM safety and measure output quality in production applications

Guardrails intervene in your LLM application's behavior based on scores from LLM judges. They run in real time before outputs reach users and can block or modify responses when scores exceed thresholds. You can use guardrails to block toxic content, filter responses for personally identifiable information (PII), or block abusive input from users.

This guide explains how Weave guardrails work, how to tune their performance, and walks through examples that use built-in scorers, custom scorers, and AWS Bedrock Guardrails to protect production LLM applications.

result.title: Score agent turns with a remote scorer
result.heading: How agent turn scoring works
result.text:
## How agent turn scoring works

An agent turn is scored in the following sequence:

1. A turn ends. When a root span (a span with no parent) ends, Weave treats it as a completed turn and emits a `weave.genai.turn_ended` event.
2. The agent scoring worker loads the project's active signals that target `weave.genai.turn_ended`, then applies each signal's filters and sample rate.
3. For each `RemoteScorer` on a matching signal, the worker builds a `schema_version: 2` request from the turn's span, including its messages, resolves the scorer's credentials, checks the endpoint URL against the allowed hosts, and sends the `POST`.
4. The worker validates the response and writes the result as feedback on the turn. Tags and ratings appear on the **Signals** tab.

Weave scores only completed turns. Individual LLM and tool spans, and whole conversations, aren't remote scoring targets. A remote scorer signal is a `Monitor` whose `op_names` is `["weave.genai.turn_ended"]`, whether you create it in the UI or with the SDK.

The worker retries a failed attempt with the same `Idempotency-Key`, up to three attempts within 30 seconds of the first attempt. A `5xx`, `408`, or `429` response is retried. A timeout uses the whole 30 seconds, so a timed-out request isn't retried. Any other `4xx` response isn't retried. If your endpoint can't score a turn in time, return `503` quickly rather than letting the request time out, so that Weave retries it. Agent turn scoring requires the structured result format, because Weave stores the tags and ratings as typed feedback columns.

result.text:
## Test the signal

Before you test, deploy the endpoint at an HTTPS URL that's on the allowed hosts, and register it.

Log one completed turn, then check the **Signals** tab. Scoring is asynchronous, so the result appears after a delay.

```python lines theme={"system"}
import uuid

from opentelemetry import trace

import weave
from weave.conversation import Message, log_turn

weave.init("[YOUR-TEAM]/[YOUR-PROJECT]")

result = log_turn(
    conversation_id=f"sample-{uuid.uuid4().hex}",
    agent_name="sample-support-agent",
    system_instructions=["Answer the user accurately and concisely."],
    messages=[Message.user("What are your support hours?")],
    output_messages=[
        Message.assistant(
            "Our support team is available Monday through Friday, 9am to 5pm Eastern."
        )
    ],
)

# weave.init exports spans from a background thread. Flush before a short script exits.
trace.get_tracer_provider().force_flush(30_000)
print(result.conversation_id, result.trace_ids)
```

Your endpoint receives a V2 request with `scoring_target.type` set to `agent_turn`, and Weave records the result as feedback on that turn.
result.page_context:
# Score agent turns with a remote scorer

> Score Weave agent turns with your own HTTP endpoint and see the results as tags or ratings on the Signals tab.

A remote scorer signal scores each completed agent turn with an HTTP endpoint that you host, instead of with an LLM judge. When a turn ends, the Weave agent scoring worker sends the turn to your endpoint in an HTTP `POST` and records the response as feedback on the turn. The result appears as a tag or rating on the **Signals** tab of the [Agents view](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-signals.md).

This page covers remote scorers for agent turns. To score Calls traced with `@weave.op`, see [Score Calls with remote scorers](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/remote-scorers.md). You configure remote scorers with the Python SDK or the Weave UI. The TypeScript SDK doesn't include `RemoteScorer`.

result.heading: How Weave guardrails work
result.text:
## How Weave guardrails work

Weave guardrails use inline [Weave Scorers](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md) to assess the input from a user or the output from an LLM and adjust the LLM's responses in real time. You can configure custom scorers or use [built-in scorers](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/builtin_scorers.md) to assess content for a variety of purposes. This guide demonstrates how to use both types of scorers as guardrails.

If you want to passively score production traffic without modifying your application's control flow, use [monitors](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/monitors.md) instead.

Unlike monitors, guardrails require code changes because they affect your application's control flow. However, every scorer result from guardrails is automatically stored in Weave's database, so your guardrails also function as monitors without any extra configuration. You can analyze historical scorer results regardless of how they were originally used.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The Weave TypeScript SDK doesn't support the tools required to set up guardrails.
result.page_context:
# Set up guardrails

> Ensure LLM safety and measure output quality in production applications

Guardrails intervene in your LLM application's behavior based on scores from LLM judges. They run in real time before outputs reach users and can block or modify responses when scores exceed thresholds. You can use guardrails to block toxic content, filter responses for personally identifiable information (PII), or block abusive input from users.

This guide explains how Weave guardrails work, how to tune their performance, and walks through examples that use built-in scorers, custom scorers, and AWS Bedrock Guardrails to protect production LLM applications.

result.heading: Key terms
result.text:
## Key terms

* **Turn**: One back-and-forth exchange between the user and the agent.
* **Rating**: A numeric score between 0.0 and 1.0 assigned to a matching span.
* **Tags**: Labels assigned to matching spans, such as "user-frustration" or "nsfw".
result.page_context:
# Monitor your agents with signals

> Use Weave signals to score agent turns, apply tags, and surface quality and safety issues in production.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/tags/create-tag.md).

In Weave's [Agents view](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-activity.md), the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations. Signals surface quality and safety issues to flag problems, find patterns, and highlight the traces that need your attention. Use signals to automatically score the quality of your agent's responses, notice when a user is frustrated, or flag NSFW content.

To score turns with an HTTP endpoint that you host instead of an LLM judge, see [Score agent turns with a remote scorer](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/remote-scorer-signals.md).

**Short answer: based on the docs I read, a Signal doesn't block anything. If you need to stop an unsafe answer before the user sees it, your application has to do that itself.**

**Why Signals aren't a gate**
- Signals show tags and ratings on your agent's conversations. They "surface quality and safety issues to flag problems, find patterns, and highlight the traces that need your attention" [S1]. That describes flagging and monitoring. The page doesn't describe blocking or changing a response.
- Agent scoring runs after a turn ends. When a root span ends, Weave treats it as a completed turn and emits a `weave.genai.turn_ended` event. A scoring worker then picks up the active signals and writes the result as feedback on the turn [S12]. The remote-scorer docs also say scoring is asynchronous, so results appear after a delay [S13]. By then the response has already been produced, so a Signal can't act as a pre-delivery check.

**What the docs say about blocking**
- Weave documents guardrails separately. They use inline Weave Scorers to assess user input or LLM output and adjust responses in real time. They can block or modify a response when a score crosses a threshold [S10][S14].
- Guardrails need code changes because they affect your application's control flow. Monitors are the alternative if you only want to score traffic passively [S14].
- Guardrail scorer results are also stored in Weave, so they work as monitors too [S14].

**Caveats**
- The guardrails page is part of the scorer and Calls workflow. I didn't find a page in the searched snapshot that wires agent Signals into a guardrail. That doesn't prove no such feature exists. It only means I couldn't confirm one.
- The guardrails page says the TypeScript SDK doesn't support the tools needed to set up guardrails [S14].

**Next step:** If you need real-time blocking, read the guardrails guide and put a scorer check in your agent's code, before it returns the response. Keep Signals for after-the-fact monitoring and triage in the Agents view.
